name: Lena Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign. What you tell me is confidential, including the part you wouldn't say at work. What does an ordinary shift look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage the returns desk for a large clothing retailer's regional office, with three people answering customers and two booking courier pickups. I got the junior manager title in July after years in customer service. I can settle an angry caller, but I still lose my place in the weekly refund figures; I ask my senior clerk to check them.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is happening at home alongside that new role?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43, have a bachelor's degree and live with my partner Pavel and our children, eight and twelve. Pavel does home-care visits, so his hours change with the rota; we have a mortgage. A roof leak used nearly all our savings and left a repair loan; we have perhaps three weeks of expenses left. My manager pay is low, and there are only a few similar offices here. I try an AI tool now and then for a draft reply, after someone else has shown me it works, but I never send the draft unchecked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our draft-reply tool could save a few minutes and the returns would still need sorting. I can handle that. The roof bill is the thing I think about when I wake up, not whether an email arrives faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my team to check a refund against the parcel scan before we send a reply. I'd tell friends the tool helps with wording, not with finding a lost coat. I wouldn't make a grand claim about AI either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm relieved about work but not about our money. Three weeks of savings is hardly a cushion when Pavel's care visits can be cancelled and the roof loan is due. I am still new at the figures, so even a quiet year needs me to improve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'd ask the senior clerk to go through the refund totals with me every Thursday, then keep the normal returns rota through the first year of a plateau. We'd stop paying for the children's streaming subscriptions for three months and send that 20 each month to the roof loan. I would keep using the draft tool only on routine replies that I check myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about our bills, though the desk itself looks steady. A quiet AI story does not refill the savings jar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the children mind losing the subscriptions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Of course. I'd explain the roof needs paying, and we'd keep the library cards and their sports days. I'm not going to pretend a 20 saving is a cure, but it is one bill we can choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What error did the clerk catch last week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I had counted a returned jacket twice because one courier scanned it at pickup and again at the depot. She showed me the two scans before I sent the report. That's why I am not letting a neat draft stand in for the actual parcel trail.

say: I'd tell the team to check **parcel scans** before sending a refund reply.
I'd tell friends the tool helps with **wording**, not with finding a lost coat.
think: I'm relieved about the desk but **anxious about bills** after the roof leak.
Three weeks saved cannot cover a bad month of **cancelled care visits**.
do: Check **refund totals** with the senior clerk every Thursday.
Pause **streaming subscriptions** for three months and put 20 monthly toward the roof loan.
Keep using **checked draft replies** only for routine customer messages.
feel: I feel **anxious** about bills while the returns desk looks steady.
S0.quote: A quiet AI story does not refill the savings jar.
fieldNote: Her **new management role** still requires help with refund totals and parcel scans.
The **thin reserve** and roof loan make her anxious even when AI changes little.
She trims **streaming costs** while keeping library access and the children's sports days.

steps.text: Check refund totals with senior clerk weekly and continue checked routine draft replies
Pause children's streaming subscriptions for three months
Send the freed 20 monthly to the roof loan for three months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Customer replies, refund checks and courier bookings are nearly my whole desk. The stronger tools in this picture could shrink our five-person group before robots move many parcels. I might be kept to handle exceptions, but a new manager with shaky figures is not the safest bet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the company and staff representatives to test the tool on missing-parcel cases, not just easy returns. I'd tell the team what the trial shows, including errors. To friends I'd say customers need a person to reach when the refund stalls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think our office hours or headcount could fall, including mine. Pavel's on-site care visits might continue longer, but the rota and records for his work can change now. His income alone won't cover the mortgage and roof loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I'd ask for an approved six-week pilot on closed missing-parcel cases and sit with the senior clerk while she shows me the tool's checks. If the manager approves, I'd use it for routine draft replies but keep a person on lost-parcel refunds and ask staff representatives to see the error count. I'd also call the roof lender about a payment schedule before a missed instalment, without assuming they'll change it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about my own hours. I could learn the tool and still be told there are fewer chairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know the pilot was safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd compare the tool's answer with the parcel scans and the actual refund date for each closed case. If it says 'refund sent' when the account wasn't credited, we'd stop using that reply. A fast wrong answer makes the next call angrier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the staff representative?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring the count of errors and ask that no hours are cut on a tidy demonstration. The staff council can ask questions I can't ask alone as a new manager. I would still be honest if the tool gets some cases right.

I'd tell friends customers need a **person to reach** when refunds stall.
think: My **own hours** could shrink with the five-person returns group.
Pavel's care wage cannot cover the **mortgage and roof loan** alone.
do: Run a **six-week closed-case pilot** if the manager approves it.
Learn the **refund checks** with the senior clerk before using routine drafts.
Ask the **staff council** to review errors before hours are cut.
feel: I feel **anxious** about losing hours even if I learn the tool.
S1.quote: I could learn the tool and still be told there are fewer chairs.
fieldNote: She is **open to tested tools**, with a senior clerk beside her for the first checks.
She separates **desk replies and bookings** from parcel handling that robots reach later.
The **mortgage and roof loan** turn even a partial hours cut into household risk.

steps.text: Learn the tool checks with the senior clerk during an approved pilot
Use AI for routine draft replies only if the manager approves
Ask staff representatives to review missing-refund errors before hours are cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If full AGI can do nearly all thinking work in 2028, it can settle the missing-parcel case too, not just write the email. The warehouse still needs people to handle returns until robots around 2031, and Pavel still visits people in their homes for now. But my desk role could go in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team the date plainly and ask for written notice and real vacancies. I'd tell Pavel we need to count what his care wage covers without my salary. In public I'd say a customer must still have a way to contest a wrong automatic refund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect to lose my returns role or most of its hours, and three weeks of savings would not cover a full month of mortgage, food, loan and bills. Pavel's care shifts are physical and may last until around 2031, but his rota and notes face AI in 2028 and his hours are never certain. I would not promise the children the house is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week Pavel and I would list mortgage, roof loan, food and his average take-home pay, then cancel the planned spring holiday before its deposit. I'd ask the staff representatives for notice and an appeal route, and start taking in two simple clothing repairs a week using the sewing machine I already own, charging only after I see whether neighbours will pay. If AGI arrives in 2028 and my desk job ends, I'd use any actual repair earnings toward food, apply for posted paid work, and ask the mortgage lender about hardship terms before missing a payment; I wouldn't budget public help until we knew we qualified.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed. My plan has small numbers because we have almost no spare money for a mistake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can two repairs a week cover the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, and I don't want to dress it up. I can shorten trousers and replace a zip, but I am not a trained tailor and neighbours may not pay me every week. It might cover some groceries while I search for a proper wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Pavel take more care visits?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd ask for open shifts, but we can't make the agency offer them. I would write the confirmed hours in our budget and leave the hoped-for ones out. The children still need one of us home after school.

say: I'd ask for **written notice and vacancies** before the returns desk is cut.
I'd insist customers can **contest wrong refunds** made by AI.
think: I expect my **desk role or hours** to go around 2028.
Three weeks saved and Pavel's variable care hours leave the **mortgage exposed**.
do: Cancel the **spring holiday** before its deposit and list fixed bills now.
Offer **two repairs weekly** using our existing sewing machine.
Ask the **lender** for hardship terms and apply for posted work if desk pay ends.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by a likely income loss and almost no cash for mistakes.
S2.quote: I would write the confirmed hours in our budget and leave the hoped-for ones out.
fieldNote: She expects **2028 desk loss**, while physical care and warehouse handling face later robots.
Her **small repair trial** cannot replace mortgage-level wages.
She counts only **confirmed care shifts** and treats support eligibility as unknown.

steps.text: Cancel the planned spring holiday before paying a deposit
Offer two simple garment repairs weekly and charge only if neighbours agree
Apply for posted paid work if the returns job ends
Ask staff representatives to seek notice and customer appeal rights

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to see whether neighbours really pay for repairs and whether I can get quicker at the refund figures while the desk still exists. AGI would take the thinking work in 2031, and robots able to handle clothes arrive around 2034. A needle in my hand is time, not a permanent shield.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my team we can ask for paid training before 2031 and a clear list of vacancies. I'd tell friends I'm testing repairs, not opening a grand shop. I would keep pressing for customer appeals when a refund is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the small repair income grows, it might pay groceries while Pavel's care wage helps with the mortgage. I still need my manager pay now, and I don't know if neighbours will bring enough work. Five years gives us a chance to pay down the roof loan before my desk changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting next January I'd take a supervised evening sewing class at the community centre only if its fee fits after the mortgage and roof payment, then practise on five donated garments. I'd keep two paid repair slots a week if customers book them and put the first 15 a week of actual earnings toward the roof loan. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, I'd apply for a posted alterations role only if its pay plus Pavel's confirmed hours covers mortgage, food and child care; otherwise I'd keep repairs small while searching other paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, but I can see a way to test the idea instead of staking the house on it. Five years is not five years of guaranteed customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you learn in the class?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn to fit a hem properly and change a zip without ruining the lining. I can do rough repairs for family. A paying customer should get neat work. I'd ask the instructor to mark each garment before I take a stranger's coat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the class fee does not fit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd keep the machine at home and do only work I know how to do. I wouldn't borrow for lessons while the roof loan is still there. We can revisit it after a month with more confirmed care shifts.

S3.quote: A paying customer should get neat work.
fieldNote: She treats **sewing as a test**, not a guaranteed new trade.
Class fees must fit after **mortgage and roof payments**, and loan repayment uses actual earnings.
A later job must cover **housing and food** plus child care alongside Pavel's confirmed hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I could become good enough at repairs to tell whether it is a real second wage. My returns desk still meets thinking AGI in 2036; robots handling clothes arrive about 2039. I'd be 53 then, with children older, but the mortgage doesn't disappear on a birthday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the company should give staff paid time to learn other work before automating the returns desk. I'd tell the council to check which promised jobs actually have wages attached. To friends I'd say ten years helps only if a household can keep paying its bills along the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might build a repair customer list and pay the roof loan off while I still have the retailer wage. That would give us a little room if the desk shrinks, though sewing could face robots around 2039 too. I wouldn't buy a bigger machine until existing repairs paid for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd ask the manager for two paid hours a month to learn garment quality checks in the returns warehouse; if approved I'd do them with the experienced checker. I'd keep taking only paid repairs I can finish after the children's school day and save the first 25 a week of actual repair earnings toward a one-month emergency account. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, I'd seek a posted alterations or garment-checking role only if its wage with Pavel's confirmed hours covers mortgage, food and child care; otherwise I'd keep the small repair work and search while robots are still about three years away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel worried, but not rushed. Ten years lets me see what customers really buy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could the warehouse quality work survive AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The reports and schedules could be automated in 2036, yes. The physical garment checks may need people until around 2039, but a manager might keep fewer checkers even before then. I would not call a shadow shift a guaranteed job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about the repair work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That it is money for the roof and the emergency jar, not a reason to give up school or family time. They can help sort buttons, but I won't build a repair business on my children's unpaid work. Our kitchen table still has to be a kitchen table.

I would not buy a new machine until **repair earnings** cover it.

Keep **paid repairs** that fit family time, saving the first 25 weekly earnings for emergencies.
Seek **posted physical garment work** after 2036 only if combined wages cover household bills.

S4.quote: I won't build a repair business on my children's unpaid work.
fieldNote: She would learn **physical garment checks**, while recognising the reports change with AGI in 2036.
She funds a **one-month emergency account** only from actual repair earnings, not hoped-for orders.
The plan protects **school and family time** while robots may reach garment handling around 2039.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my returns desk could close before the roof loan is paid, and Pavel's hours cannot carry the mortgage alone. I'd want a dated notice, paid training attached to an actual vacancy, and a right for customers and workers to challenge wrong automatic decisions. If income support exists and we qualify, that could bridge a gap, but I wouldn't put it in our budget before seeing the rules.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays when a coat is marked returned but never reaches the warehouse. The customer thinks we're holding their money, and my team has to find the missing parcel. A perfect reply is no use when the refund is still missing.

headlineQuote: A perfect reply is no use when the refund is still missing.
portrait: Lena, **43**, became a junior returns manager at a large clothing retailer and checks refund figures with a senior clerk.
Her **low manager pay** and Pavel's variable home-care hours support two school-age children and a mortgage.
A roof leak left about **three weeks saved**, with few similar offices nearby; she sometimes uses AI drafts after colleagues test them.
She would try **verified tools** and garment repairs for income, while asking staff representatives for notice and a way to challenge errors.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could close the returns desk before the roof loan is paid or another wage is secured.
whatWouldHelp: **Dated notice** and paid training linked to a real vacancy before wages end.
A **challenge route** for wrong decisions and income help only if her family qualifies.
